The Euclid syllabus tests polynomials as part of a wider algebra strand that also includes basic algebraic manipulation and simultaneous equations, sequences, coordinate geometry, plane geometry, number theory, trigonometric identities and equations, counting and probability, and exponentials and logarithms. ... ## Practice Plan: Pair Theorem-Based Proofs With Selected Polynomial Questions\\n\\nThe theorem earns its keep in two situations. First, when a question gives remainders and asks for unknown coefficients, it turns each remainder directly into an equation. Second, when you want to test whether a candidate value of a parameter is consistent, it converts a division into a substitution, which is far less error-prone under time pressure.\\n\\nIt is equally worth knowing what the theorem does not do. It does not produce the quotient Q(x). If the question asks for the quotient as well, you still have to divide, and you should say how. And for a divisor of degree two or higher, the remainder is not a single number but a polynomial of degree lower than the divisor, so one substitution usually will not determine it. In that case either perform the division, or substitute several values of x that make the divisor zero, if such values exist.\\n\\nWorked illustration (a teaching example, not a past contest problem). Suppose P(x) = x³ + kx – 4 is divided by (x – 1) and the remainder is 0. By the Remainder Theorem, P(1) = 0. Substituting: 1³ + k(1) – 4 = 0, so 1 + k – 4 = 0 and k = 3. Check: P(x) = x³ + 3x – 4, and P(1) = 1 + 3 – 4 = 0. The answer is k = 3, and the justification is the named theorem plus the shown substitution. Neither half of that pair is optional in a written solution.\\n\\n## Factor Theorem: Turning a Known Root into a Divisor Without Long Division\\n\\nThe Factor Theorem is the Remainder Theorem read in the other direction: (x – a) is a factor of P(x) if and only if P(a) = 0. Because the statement runs both ways, it does two jobs. Reading it left to right, it tells you that if (x – a) is already known to be a factor, then P(a) must be zero. Reading it right to left, it tells you that if you evaluate P(a) and get zero, then (x – a) is a factor, and therefore you may write P(x) = (x – a)Q(x) for some polynomial Q whose degree is one less than the degree of P.\\n\\nThe second direction is the workhorse. Once you have written P(x) = (x – a)Q(x), the problem has shrunk: you have removed one root and reduced the degree by one. For a cubic, that leaves a quadratic, which you may be able to factor by inspection or handle with the quadratic formula. For a quartic, you may be able to apply the process again with a second root, whether given in the question or discovered during the work.\\n\\nFor a stated factor, the safest wording is: since P(a) = 0, the Factor Theorem gives that (x – a) is a factor of P(x), so P(x) = (x – a)Q(x). Then show how Q was obtained, either by writing out the division or by stating the quotient you found together with how you verified it. The Factor Theorem does not hand you the quotient; it hands you the right to look for one.\\n\\nSigns are the most common place this goes wrong. The factor corresponding to the root a is (x – a), not (x + a). If the root is -3, the factor is (x + 3). Write the root and the factor on the same line so the correspondence is visible: P(-3) = 0, so (x + 3) is a factor. If you substitute first and only afterwards decide what the factor should be, check the sign again before you divide.\\n\\n## Labelled Teaching Illustration: The Theorem-to-Quotient Chain\\n\\nSuppose, for illustration only, that P(x) = x³ – 6x² + 11x – 6 and that we are told P(1) = 0. This is a textbook cubic, used here to show the writing pattern rather than to reproduce any Euclid question. The chain runs in three steps.\\n\\nStep 1, apply the Factor Theorem. Since P(1) = 0, the Factor Theorem gives that (x – 1) is a factor of P(x), so P(x) = (x – 1)Q(x) for some quadratic Q.\\n\\nStep 2, find the quotient. Divide x³ – 6x² + 11x – 6 by (x – 1). Synthetic division using the coefficients 1, -6, 11, -6 and the root 1 gives: bring down 1; multiply 1 by 1 and add to -6 to get -5; multiply -5 by 1 and add to 11 to get 6; multiply 6 by 1 and add to -6 to get 0. The quotient is Q(x) = x² – 5x + 6 and the remainder is 0, which is what the Factor Theorem predicted.\\n\\nStep 3, factor the quadratic. x² – 5x + 6 factors as (x – 2)(x – 3), since 2 and 3 multiply to 6 and add to 5. Combining the results gives P(x) = (x – 1)(x – 2)(x – 3).\\n\\nThe value of this sequence is not the answer. The answer could be reached by inspection. The value is the written chain. Every line uses the previous line. Every factor is justified by a stated condition. The last step is a genuine simplification rather than an assertion. That is the shape a full-solution marker is looking for, and it is the shape that transfers directly to harder polynomial questions where the algebra cannot be done in your head.\\n\\n## Diagnostic: Three Prompts That Test Whether You Name the Conditions\\n\\nBefore you conclude any polynomial solution, run three quick questions against the page in front of you.\\n\\nFirst, did I state which theorem applies before using it? A solution that jumps from P(2) = 0 straight to ‘therefore (x – 2) is a factor’ has used the Factor Theorem without naming it, and the reader has to supply the reason.\\n\\nSecond, did I identify the divisor or the root explicitly? The value a in P(a) and the divisor (x – a) both need to appear, and the substitution needs to be visible, not implied.\\n\\nThird, did I explain why a zero remainder implies a factor? A zero remainder means the divisor divides P(x) exactly, which is precisely the content of the Factor Theorem.
